lines.text: If humans had never gotten used to wearing clothes, getting ready in the morning would take about ten seconds.
lines.caption: If humans had never gotten used to wearing clothes, getting ready in the morning would take about 10 seconds.

lines.text: No outfit to pick, nothing to iron, and no missing socks.
Your walk-in closet? That's a walk-in pantry now.
But there'd be one big problem: no clothes means no pockets.
So everyone would wear a fanny pack, making it the best-selling accessory on the planet.
Fashion wouldn't disappear, though. It would just move onto your skin.
Body paint, glitter and tattoos would replace outfits, and the biggest trend of the year might be a painted-on tuxedo.
Uniforms would shrink to the bare minimum. A police officer would just be a hat and a badge.
A chef would be a hat and an apron.
And for some reason, your boss would still wear a tie.
It's called being professional.
Scientists think humans started wearing clothes as early as a hundred and seventy thousand years ago.
lines.caption: Scientists think humans started wearing clothes as early as 170,000 years ago.

lines.text: And the weird part? We know that because of lice.
You see, body lice can only live in clothing, and their DNA shows they split from head lice right around that time.
Even then, some people skipped them. In ancient Greece, athletes competed completely naked.
The word gymnasium even comes from the Greek word for naked.
Legend says it started when a runner's loincloth fell off mid-race... and he won.
Back in our world, every bus seat would come with a towel dispenser.
Because the number one rule at real nudist resorts is: always sit on a towel.
lines.caption: Because the #1 rule at real nudist resorts is: always sit on a towel.

lines.text: And there'd be sunscreen stations on every corner, because covering your whole body takes a shot glass of sunscreen, every two hours.
lines.caption: And there'd be sunscreen stations on every corner, because covering your whole body takes a shot glass of sunscreen, every 2 hours.

lines.text: At work, the dress code would just be a name tag.
And the office thermostat war would finally end, because without clothes, most people are comfortable at about eighty-two degrees.
lines.caption: And the office thermostat war would finally end, because without clothes, most people are comfortable at about 82 degrees.

lines.text: Which is great for your coworkers, and terrible for the heating bill.
Meanwhile, the clothing industry, worth about one point seven trillion dollars a year, would almost completely disappear.
lines.caption: Meanwhile, the clothing industry, worth about $1.7 trillion a year, would almost completely disappear.

lines.text: And the planet would get a break. Making one cotton T-shirt takes about two thousand seven hundred liters of water.
lines.caption: And the planet would get a break. Making one cotton T-shirt takes about 2,700 liters of water.

lines.text: That's enough drinking water for one person for two and a half years.
lines.caption: That's enough drinking water for one person for 2.5 years.

lines.text: But it wouldn't all be great. Cooking bacon would become an extreme sport.
Which is why aprons would be the one piece of clothing everybody owns.
In cold countries, coats would work like umbrellas. You'd wear one outside, and drop it the second you got in.
Invited to a fancy dinner? You'd dress up by wearing... a nice watch.
And anyone who showed up fully dressed would get stared at, like they'd worn a Halloween costume to dinner.
Is this... not the costume party?
Laundry would basically disappear. The average family washes about three hundred loads a year. Now it would just be towels.
lines.caption: Laundry would basically disappear. The average family washes about 300 loads a year. Now it would just be towels.

lines.text: And getting ready for bed would take exactly zero seconds.
lines.caption: And getting ready for bed would take exactly 0 seconds.

lines.text: In fact, the only one in your house still wearing clothes... would be your dog.
